newsitem.title: USA: Fargo battles rising Red River.
newsitem.headline: Fargo battles rising Red River.

text.p: Hundreds of college and high school students left their classrooms on Tuesday to join a volunteer force fighting a steadily rising Red River that has swamped hundreds of homes in the worst flood in 100 years.

"It's very serious and they (flood experts) are quite concerned," Fargo Mayor Bruce Furness told a news conference as the Red continued to rise at the rate of a half-inch an hour in North Dakota's largest city.
He said permanent levees and private dikes were holding but hot spots were developong all over town and around-the-clock sandbag repairs were needed.
"We're going to get up there at higher numbers longer than anybody anticipated," Dennis Walaker, operations director for the city's Public Works department, said.
"We are expecting the Red to go up at least another half foot. We are still ahead of the game but we are seeing some things we have never seen before," he said.

One unprecedented development, he said, is that the Red may crest all at once as a vast lake along a 128-mile stretch from Wahpeton south of Fargo to Grand Forks on the north because so much water was being released from melting snow as the weather got warmer.
Normally the water would peak first at Wahpeton, then at Fargo and several days later at Grand Forks as the northward-flowing Red moves into Canada.
At mid-morning on Tuesday the Red had reached 37.9 feet in Fargo, more than 20 feet over flood stage and the highest level recorded since a devastating flood in April 1897.

Students from North Dakota State University, Concordia College and Moorhead State University left classes to heed appeals for sadgbag filling. Area high school students were also allowed to leave school to help.
In Cass County, north of Fargo, emergency management director Glenn Ellingsberg expressed fears that more farms and rural subdivisions would be innundated by waters creeping across the flat farmland.
He urged residents needing to be evacuated to contact officials during the day since Coast Guard units face danger and confusion trying to remove people after dark.
A Coast Guard helicopter on Monday night plucked a family of six from their home near Hillsboro.
"We have had several sorties...and are getting requests for helicopter and boat rescues," said Bill Stouder, a Coast Guard spokesman in Bismarck.
In Breckenridge, Minnesota, a city of 4,000 south of Fargo and upstream on the Red, the Boise De Sioux River, a tributary of the Red, burst through a dike on Monday night.
"We lost the southside last (Monday) night. It (the river) spilled into a residential area," said Wilkin County Emergency Services Director Jack Thompson. "We are evacuating it now."
Fargo's Walaker said, "You really have to search to find any positive news today ... the warming temperatures have basically taken the rest of the snowpack and the ice and turned it into water."
